name: Sprint/HIIT for growth hormone

card.summary: Sprints and HIIT do raise growth hormone briefly, but no trial shows they add height.
card.note: Exercise-induced GH rises are temporary; no study links them to final height.

quick.overview:
Some teens do sprints or interval training because intense exercise raises growth hormone, which is involved in childhood growth.

The exercise-GH link is documented, but no published trial has tested whether such workouts change adult height.
quick.mechanism: Vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH pulses, and GH acts on growth cartilage directly and through IGF-1. Believers extend this to a height effect; reference sources do not report that extension.
quick.risks: Sprint and interval training carry the usual risks of high-intensity exercise such as muscle and tendon strain. Adult height is described as largely genetic, with nutrition and health as the main modifiable factors.

lead: Sprint or high-intensity interval training (HIIT) for growth hormone is a height-related practice in which teenagers do all-out sprints or interval workouts in the belief that the resulting surge in growth hormone (GH) will help them grow taller or look more developed. It rests on the fact that vigorous exercise is a recognised stimulus of GH secretion, and GH is the hormone best known for its role in childhood growth.[1]

Wikipedia describes increased childhood height as GH's most widely known effect, working both directly on cartilage cells and through IGF-1 made mainly in the liver, and notes that young adolescents secrete roughly 700 micrograms a day versus about 400 in healthy adults.[1] HIIT itself is a training format that alternates short, intense anaerobic efforts with brief recoveries, and the same encyclopedia entry reports that in adolescents it can increase muscle mass, especially in the mid-to-late teens, and can reduce body fat in youth with obesity.[3] For appearance, that gives the practice a second payoff alongside the height hope: a leaner, more muscular build.

Adult height is described as largely heritable, with nutrition and health in childhood the main environmental factors.[2] No published trial has tested sprint or HIIT training as a way to change final height in healthy adolescents.

chain: Sprints and intervals stimulate GH release
GH and IGF-1 support growth in the growing years
Taller frame (as practitioners hope), plus leaner, more muscular build
angle.text: Practitioners use sprints and interval circuits to trigger natural GH pulses while growth plates are still open. Separately, HIIT is documented to build fitness and, in teens, muscle and lower body fat, which changes how the body looks.

infobox: Short maximal sprints or interval circuits

paras: Practitioners describe short, maximal-effort sprints, hill sprints or interval circuits performed several times a week, sometimes combined with sleep and nutrition routines, with the stated aim of maximising natural GH release during the years when growth is still possible.
Wikipedia describes HIIT as alternating short intense bursts with brief recovery, with sessions typically under 30 minutes and a common ratio of about 2:1 work to rest.[3]

GH is released in pulses. Wikipedia lists sleep, vigorous exercise, fasting, sex hormones in puberty, ghrelin and others among stimulators, and describes the largest daily peak as occurring about an hour after sleep onset.[1] In children, GH deficiency causes growth failure and short stature, which underlies the idea that more GH could mean more height.[1]

Twin studies cited by Wikipedia estimate that 60 to 80 percent of height variation within a population is heritable, and growth reaches zero on average around 15 to 16 in females and 18 to 19 in males.[2] Chronic malnutrition during childhood is associated with reduced adult height.[2]

Wikipedia reports HIIT modestly reduces subcutaneous fat in healthy people and more in overweight people, and that in teens 8 to 12 weeks of HIIT combined with resistance training reduced waist size and body fat percentage in a 2021 review.[3] It also notes HIIT may be less effective than longer sessions for building muscle or bone mass.[3]
No studies found on sprint or HIIT training and final height in adolescents. Reference sources note that exercise raises GH levels temporarily.[1]

lore.intro: In height-focused forum discussion, sprinting and HIIT are often listed among free ways to support growth during puberty.

claims.claim: Sprinting spikes GH, so it makes teens taller
claims.believers: Proponents point to the well-known exercise-induced GH rise and argue that more GH pulses during puberty should translate to extra growth.
claims.experts: Reference sources confirm that vigorous exercise stimulates GH secretion but do not report that this changes final height; no trial has tested the question.[1][2]

claims.claim: HIIT in the teens builds a leaner, more athletic physique
claims.believers: Practitioners present interval work as a time-efficient way to lose fat and gain athletic conditioning.
claims.experts: Reviews summarised by Wikipedia report reduced body fat and increased muscle mass in adolescents on HIIT programmes.[3]
